content: The Herxheimer reaction, which can occur during the treatment of conditions such as Lyme disease and relapsing fever, typically begins within one to two hours after therapy initiation and resolves within 12 to 24 hours. This reaction is characterized by symptoms including fever, chills, muscle pain (myalgias), headache, worsening of skin lesions, rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), increased breathing rate (hyperventilation), skin flushing due to vasodilation, and mild low blood pressure (hypotension). The underlying mechanism of the Herxheimer reaction is thought to involve the release of host-stable pyrogens from the spirochetes. Penicillin hypersensitivity is often the result of prior exposure to the drug, although immediate allergic reactions have been observed in individuals receiving penicillin for the first time. It is hypothesized that prior exposure may have occurred through trace amounts of penicillin present in milk or vaccines. Clinically, two types of allergic reactions to penicillin are recognized: immediate and delayed. Immediate allergic reactions typically occur within 20 minutes of administration and can range in severity from hives (urticaria) and itching (pruritus) to more severe manifestations such as angioedema, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, low blood pressure (hypotension), vascular collapse, and even death. These anaphylactic reactions are rare and are more commonly associated with parenteral (injected) therapy, though cases have also been reported following oral administration. Another form of immediate reaction, known as an accelerated reaction, may occur between 20 minutes and 45 hours after administration and can include symptoms such as hives, itching, fever, and occasionally laryngeal edema. Delayed allergic reactions to penicillin therapy usually develop within one to two weeks after starting treatment. These reactions may present with fever, general discomfort (malaise), hives, muscle pain, joint pain, abdominal pain, and various skin rashes, ranging from maculopapular eruptions to severe exfoliative dermatitis. Contact dermatitis has also been observed in individuals handling penicillin solutions. In the gastrointestinal system, pseudomembranous colitis has been reported during or after penicillin G treatment. Other symptoms of gastrointestinal irritation, such as nausea, vomiting, inflammation of the mouth (stomatitis), and discoloration of the tongue (black or hairy tongue), may occur, particularly with oral therapy. Hematologic reactions include neutropenia, which resolves after discontinuation of penicillin therapy. Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia, a rare reaction, has been observed in patients receiving high doses of intravenous penicillin G (greater than 10 million units per day) who have previously been exposed to large doses of the drug. Additionally, high doses of penicillin can lead to bleeding disorders due to platelet dysfunction. Intravenous administration of large doses of penicillin G sodium (containing 68 mEq of sodium ion) may result in serious and potentially fatal electrolyte imbalances. In the cardiovascular system, high doses of penicillin G sodium can lead to congestive heart failure due to excessive sodium intake. Neurologic side effects, including hyperreflexia, myoclonic twitches, seizures, and coma, have been reported following the administration of massive intravenous doses of penicillin. These effects are more likely to occur in patients with impaired renal function. In the urogenital system, renal tubular damage and interstitial nephritis have been associated with large intravenous doses of penicillin G. Symptoms of this reaction may include fever, rash, elevated eosinophil count (eosinophilia), protein in the urine (proteinuria), eosinophils in the urine (eosinophiluria), blood in the urine (hematuria), and increased serum urea nitrogen levels. Discontinuation of penicillin G typically leads to resolution of these symptoms in most patients. Local reactions, such as phlebitis and thrombophlebitis, may occur with intravenous administration of penicillin.
